title: An infinity sign is called a “lemniscate.”
fact: The term refers to a plane curve in which two loops meet at a central point, forming a sideways figure-eight. Derived from the Latin word for 'with hanging ribbons'.

title: The longest English word is nearly 190,000 letters.
fact: It’s the chemical name of Titin, the largest known protein, starting with 'Methionylthreonylthreonyl...' and stretching for tens of thousands of letters.

title: The longest word in a major dictionary has 45 letters.
fact: ‘Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis’ refers to a lung disease caused by silica dust. It was coined in the 1930s just to become the longest word.

title: The word 'bankrupt' means 'broken bench'.
fact: From Italian 'banca rotta', meaning ‘broken bench’ — an old custom where a money dealer’s bench was broken when they lost their funds.

title: There’s a word for all things breakfast.
fact: ‘Jentacular’ means ‘pertaining to breakfast’.

title: The word 'heroin' was trademarked by Bayer.
fact: Bayer sold heroin as an over-the-counter drug in the late 19th century. The name came from the German word 'heroisch' (powerful).

title: A single piece of confetti is a 'confetto'.
fact: ‘Confetti’ is plural; one piece is a ‘confetto’.

title: ‘Schoolmaster’ is an anagram of ‘the classroom’.
fact: Other examples include 'Astronomers' = 'Moon starers' and 'Clint Eastwood' = 'Old West Action'.

title: ‘Walrus’ may mean ‘whale-horse’.
fact: It comes from Old English 'horschwael', literally meaning 'horse whale'.

title: ‘Penguin’ means ‘white head’.
fact: Derived from Welsh 'pen' (head) and 'gwyn' (white). Originally referred to the now-extinct great auk.

title: ‘Adultery’ and ‘adult’ have different origins.
fact: ‘Adult’ comes from Latin 'adolescere' (to grow up); ‘adultery’ comes from 'adulterare' (to corrupt).

title: ‘Crwth’ and ‘cwtch’ are words without vowels.
fact: Both are Welsh words that treat ‘w’ as a vowel.

title: There’s a word for 'the day before yesterday'.
fact: ‘Nudiustertian’ means the day before yesterday.

title: ‘Ambulance’ means 'walking hospital'.
fact: From Latin 'ambulare' (to walk); Napoleon used 'hopital ambulant' for mobile battlefield hospitals.

title: ‘Funk’ originated in Elizabethan England.
fact: From Old French 'funkier', meaning 'to blow smoke on'. Originally described a musty smell.

title: ‘Bogus’ was once a noun.
fact: Originally referred to a counterfeit coin-making machine.

title: The opposite of déjà vu is ‘jamais vu’.
fact: French for 'never seen', describing when something familiar feels foreign.

title: ‘Bellwether’ comes from sheep herding.
fact: A bell was hung on the lead sheep (‘wether’), which guided the rest.

title: Only one English word has X, Y, and Z in order.
fact: That word is ‘hydroxyzine’, an antihistamine medication.

title: ‘Pandemonium’ was invented by John Milton.
fact: He coined it in ‘Paradise Lost’ as the name of Hell’s capital.
